1: # AGENTS.md — 01_Ideas
2: 
3: Raw, unstructured concept capture. Low friction — just enough context to remember.
4: 
5: ## Why have ideas?
6: 
7: To capture every thought about the homelab before it's lost. Ideas are the seed of the pipeline — no idea is too small or too vague.
8: 
9: ## When to create
10: 
11: Any thought about new tech, homelab changes, or wishlist items.
12: 
13: ## Status Lifecycle
14: 
15: ```
16: draft → accepted
17:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/ideas/)
18: ```
19: 
20: - **draft**: Just captured
21: - **accepted**: Worth pursuing
22: - **archived**: Discarded or superseded
23: 
24: ## File system layout
25: 
26: ```
27: 01_Ideas/{topic}/
28: ├── idea-{name}.md     # one per specific idea
29: ├── idea-notes.md      # scratchpad, raw thoughts, links
30: └── overview.md        # high-level summary of the topic area
31: ```
32: 
33: All names in kebab-case. Multiple files per topic allowed. Use the atomic rule (150 lines) to decide when to split.
34: 
35: ## Frontmatter (required)
36: 
37: ```yaml
38: ---
39: title: ""
40: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
41: author: ""
42: date: YYYY-MM-DD
43: tags: []
44: technologies: []
45: related_ideas: []
46: ---
47: ```
48: 
49: Example:
50: 
51: ```yaml
52: ---
53: title: "Move databases to separate node"
54: status: draft
55: author: "padawont"
56: date: 2026-08-13
57: tags: [databases, performance, architecture]
58: technologies: [postgresql, mysql, mariadb]
59: related_ideas: []
60: ---
61: ```
62: 
63: See `./Templates/ideas/idea.md` for a copyable template.
64: 
65: ## Structure
66: 
67: No strict structure — freeform markdown. The template provides a starting point.
68: 
69: ## Conventions
70: 
71: - No formal review needed for `draft → accepted`
72: - No stale timeout — ideas live indefinitely
73: - When `accepted`, the idea is ready — optionally create a Knowledge note
74: - Use `idea-notes.md` for loose thoughts that don't warrant their own file

11: # Evaluate Open Knowledge Format for the PKM
12: 
13: ## Objective
14: 
15: Evaluate the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) as validation and inspiration for the
16: Homelab PKM's own format design. OKF stores knowledge as plain markdown files
17: with YAML frontmatter in a git-versioned directory hierarchy — the same core
18: design this repo already uses (see `AGENTS.md`).
19: 
20: ## Possibilities
21: 
22: - **Borrow OKF's trust/provenance signals in frontmatter**: `sources` with
23:   per-source credibility, `verified`/`generated`, `status` + `stale_after` so
24:   an agent-maintained corpus stays trustable without a runtime.
25: - **Auto-generated `index.md` per directory** for progressive disclosure — an
26:   agent or human navigates one level at a time instead of loading everything
27:   into context.
28: - **Graph-shaped cross-linking** beyond the folder tree: concepts link to each
29:   other via normal markdown links, not just parent/child directories.
30: - **Secondary tooling idea**: `kcmd` (Metadata-as-Code, from the
31:   knowledge-catalog repo) manages metadata as source artifacts with pull/push
32:   sync and ships an MCP server — a possible pattern for homelab metadata
33:   management.
34: 
35: ## Open Questions
36: 
37: - Is the OKF v0.2 spec stable/mature enough to depend on, or still moving?
38: - Does adopting OKF-style fields conflict with the frontmatter conventions
39:   already defined per-section in the AGENTS.md files?
40: - Is the OKF reference agent practical to run in a homelab (BigQuery + Gemini
41:   dependencies), or is the format the only useful part?
42: - Is `stale_after` freshness worth adding to this PKM's knowledge notes, or
43:   does the existing `last_audit_date` convention suffice?
44: 
45: ## Sources
46: 
47: - OKF canonical repo (the `knowledge-catalog` copy is a frozen snapshot):
48:   <https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format>
49: - OKF spec v0.2 snapshot and tooling:
50:   <https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog>

# Expose the NAS only through a zero-trust proxy

## Access model

Reach the NAS exclusively through an identity-aware proxy instead of the
network edge. No port forwards are opened on the router; every request is
authenticated and authorized at the proxy before it reaches the NAS. Policy is
defined per app rather than per network segment, so each service behind the
proxy gets its own access rule and identity requirement.
